text: You've got six real artifacts from this path. This lesson is about turning them into a resume that actually gets read — by a human, and by whatever keyword-matching system stands between you and that human.

A line like 'results-driven IT professional with strong technical skills' tells a recruiter nothing they can match against a requisition. A ServiceNow resume needs specific platform vocabulary right at the top: which modules you've configured, which scripting constructs you can write — Business Rules, Client Scripts, Script Includes — and which integration tools you've used. 'Configured Incident and Change workflows; built a four-step Flow Designer approval flow; wrote Script Includes to extend a scoped application' does more work in three lines than a paragraph of summary language does in ten.

Each resume bullet should name what you built, the specific capability it demonstrates, and the outcome in honest terms. Here's the part to get right: it's tempting to invent a number, like 'reduced ticket resolution time by forty percent.' But these are lab and capstone projects on a Personal Developer Instance, with no real users and no real baseline — that number can't be backed up, and a good interviewer will ask how you measured it. The honest version is a structural claim: 'reduced manual ticket-routing steps by automating approval and assignment logic in Flow Designer.' True, specific, and defensible, without a fabricated metric.

The same honesty applies to certifications still in progress. List CSA or CAD as 'in progress' if that's where you actually are — don't list it as earned, and don't leave it off the resume either, since an in-progress certification still signals real, active commitment to the platform. That gap gets caught the moment someone checks ServiceNow's own verification tool, and it costs far more credibility than simply being honest about exactly where you stand.
Specific capabilities, structural outcomes, honest certification status. Next up: taking one of these artifacts and writing it up as a full portfolio document that survives real interview questions.
